nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
Thinking can be useful long before it feels pleasant. The question is whether the next round of thought changes what you know or what you can do.

When does trying to solve a problem turn into staying stuck with it?
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

nodes.title: What planning means

Thinking that produces a specific next step, decision or test.

nodes.title: What rumination means
nodes.body:
Returning repeatedly to distressing questions or past events without making progress.

For example: After a conversation, someone replays the same sentence to work out whether they seemed foolish.

One important limit: Reflection can lead to learning when it reaches a new conclusion or action.

Repeating an action to gain confidence or temporary relief from uncertainty.

For example: A student rereads an unchanged email draft fifteen times before sending it.

One important limit: Checking may be sensible when it actually catches errors; look at the information gained and the cost.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Jo has an interview on Friday. Amir finds her repeatedly rewriting the same answer to a question she already prepared.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.
nodes.scenario: Jo has an interview on Friday. Amir finds her repeatedly rewriting the same answer to a question she already prepared.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Are you still working on the interview answers?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I've rewritten this one six times. I think I can make it safer.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: What specifically was wrong with the last version?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I don't know. Someone could misunderstand it.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.
checks.counterexample: Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

items.label: “Are you still working on the interview answers?”
Jo's repeated revision may be driven by intolerance of uncertainty. Editing temporarily lowers discomfort, but without a stopping rule the sense of risk returns.
“I've rewritten this one six times. I think I can make it safer.”
Jo could be addressing genuine weaknesses in her answer, particularly if each revision improves clarity or performance.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Jo's repeated revision may be driven by intolerance of uncertainty. Editing temporarily lowers discomfort, but without a stopping rule the sense of risk returns.

Another possibility: Jo could be addressing genuine weaknesses in her answer, particularly if each revision improves clarity or performance.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Look for a defined question, a stopping point and measurable improvement between revisions. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Look for a defined question, a stopping point and measurable improvement between revisions.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Jo's first mock-interview performance was strong. On the following night she spent another three hours altering wording without testing the changes.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The lack of new feedback strengthens the hypothesis that revision has become a way to manage anxiety rather than improve the answer.
nodes.counterexample: Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Preparation that stops preparing you
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and Unconstructive Repetitive Thought.
nodes.scenario: Rae has an interview tomorrow and has revised the same answer several times.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I've rewritten my opening answer six times.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you tried saying it aloud?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Once. Every time I rehearse, I find another thing to worry about.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Does a new rewrite change anything you'll actually say?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It might. If I keep refining it, they won't catch me out.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What information would tell you that further rewriting is no longer useful?

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: The answer still contains substantial factual mistakes that further preparation could correct.
Rae finds writing more effective than speaking because the interview will be written.
Rae may be using repeated revision to gain a feeling of certainty rather than to improve performance.
Jo may fear how she will be judged more than the accuracy of the answer itself.
options.feedback: This could be part of the process, though it does not by itself explain why repeated editing feels briefly relieving.

options.label: Jo may have learned from past interviews that minor wording differences influence outcomes.
options.feedback: Prior feedback would matter, but no such evidence is offered for these particular changes.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Rae may be using repeated revision to gain a feeling of certainty rather than to improve performance. The answer still contains substantial factual mistakes that further preparation could correct. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Further preparation is rational when there is a genuine knowledge gap. The difference is whether the next round of thinking can change a decision or action.

checks.prompt: You are Rae. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Say one answer aloud, note one specific improvement and rehearse the changed version.
options.reply: Then the search changed your anxiety more than your readiness.
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Rewrite until you feel certain you have covered every possible question.
options.reply: What information would tell you that further rewriting is no longer useful?
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: Does a new rewrite change anything you'll actually say?
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: Did you learn something you can use?
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: Jo may fear how she will be judged more than the accuracy of the answer itself.
options.feedback: This could be part of the process, though it does not by itself explain why repeated editing feels briefly relieving.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Jo's repeated revision may be driven by intolerance of uncertainty. Editing temporarily lowers discomfort, but without a stopping rule the sense of risk returns.

Long thinking is not necessarily rumination. The distinction lies in whether it produces new information or useful action relative to its costs.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Watkins (2008), Constructive and unconstructive repetitive thought; Borkovec et al., worry and avoidance.

glossary.definition: Thinking that produces a specific next step, decision or test.
glossary.example: After practising an interview answer, someone decides which example to use.
glossary.limit: A plan can still be imperfect; certainty is not a requirement.

glossary.definition: Repeated thinking about possible future problems, often when an outcome cannot yet be known.
glossary.example: Someone keeps imagining every question an interviewer might ask.
glossary.limit: Preparing for a realistic risk differs from endlessly searching for impossible certainty.

glossary.definition: Returning repeatedly to distressing questions or past events without making progress.
glossary.example: After a conversation, someone replays the same sentence to work out whether they seemed foolish.
glossary.limit: Reflection can lead to learning when it reaches a new conclusion or action.

glossary.definition: Repeating an action to gain confidence or temporary relief from uncertainty.
glossary.example: A student rereads an unchanged email draft fifteen times before sending it.
glossary.limit: Checking may be sensible when it actually catches errors; look at the information gained and the cost.
